title: Free Will and Determinism
subtitle: Could you have done otherwise, and does it matter?
objectives: By the end you will be able to define determinism and distinguish hard determinism, libertarianism and compatibilism.
By the end you will be able to reconstruct the Consequence Argument and the luck objection to libertarianism.
By the end you will be able to explain Frankfurt cases and Frankfurt's hierarchical theory of freedom of the will.
By the end you will be able to describe the Libet experiments and evaluate what neuroscience does and does not show about free will.
hook:
This morning you chose what to eat for breakfast. It felt like a choice: you could have had toast; you went for cereal. But think about what produced that choice: your hunger, your habits, the contents of your cupboard, the state of your neurons, each caused by earlier events reaching back before your birth. If all of that fixed what you would do, in what sense could you have done otherwise?

In the Ethics track's lesson on moral luck you met **causal luck**, the possibility that everything we do is the product of factors beyond our control. You have also met Spinoza (Day 45), who denied free will, Hume (Day 49), who argued that freedom is compatible with necessity, and Sartre (Day 77), who held that we are "condemned to be free." This lesson sets out the modern debate with precision: three positions, two powerful arguments, an ingenious set of thought experiments, and the neuroscience experiments that are often said to have settled the matter, though they have not.

sections.heading: Determinism and the Three Positions
sections.body:
**Determinism** is the thesis that the state of the world at any one time, together with the laws of nature, fixes a unique future. Given the past and the laws, only one outcome is possible. In 1814 Pierre-Simon Laplace gave the idea a famous image: an intellect that knew, at one instant, all the forces of nature and the positions of all things, and could analyze this data, would be able to predict the entire future and retrodict the entire past. This is **Laplace's demon**.

Note what determinism is *not*. It is not **fatalism**, the idea that some outcome will happen whatever you do. Determinism says your choices make a difference: they are links in the causal chain. It is also not the claim that we can *predict* everything; a deterministic system can be unpredictable in practice, as chaos theory shows.

Is determinism true? Physics does not settle the matter. On standard interpretations of quantum mechanics, some events at the microscopic level are genuinely random. But other interpretations are deterministic, and it is unclear whether quantum randomness affects decisions made by brains. Philosophers therefore ask a conditional question: *if* determinism were true, could we have free will?

This yields the basic map.
- **Incompatibilists** say free will and determinism cannot both be true. They split into two camps.
- **Hard determinists** (or, more broadly, **free will skeptics**) are incompatibilists who accept determinism, or at least deny we have the kind of control needed for free will. Spinoza (Day 45) and Baron d'Holbach in the eighteenth century held views of this kind; Derk Pereboom and Gregg Caruso defend skepticism today.
- **Libertarians** (no relation to the political view) are incompatibilists who hold that we have free will, so determinism is false, at least for human choices.
- **Compatibilists** hold that free will and determinism are compatible. Hobbes and Hume (Day 49) held versions of this view, and it is the majority position among professional philosophers today: in the 2020 PhilPapers survey, around 59 percent accepted or leaned toward compatibilism.

The word **free will** itself is contested. A useful working definition: free will is the kind of control over our actions that is required for **moral responsibility**, in particular for deserving praise and blame. This links the debate directly to Strawson's reactive attitudes (Ethics, Lesson 3).

sections.heading: The Consequence Argument and Libertarian Freedom
sections.body:
The strongest argument for incompatibilism is the **Consequence Argument**, given its classic form by Peter van Inwagen in *An Essay on Free Will* (1983). Informally:

1. If determinism is true, our acts are the consequences of the laws of nature and events in the remote past.
2. We have no choice about what went on before we were born.
3. We have no choice about what the laws of nature are.
4. If we have no choice about something, and no choice about the fact that it leads to something else, then we have no choice about that something else.
5. Therefore, if determinism is true, we have no choice about our present acts.

Premise 4, the **transfer principle** (van Inwagen's "Rule Beta"), says that powerlessness transfers along chains of consequences. It is plausible: if I have no choice about whether the Sun rises, and no choice about the fact that the Sun's rising wakes me, then I have no choice about whether I wake. Compatibilists usually attack this premise, or argue that "could have done otherwise" means something weaker than van Inwagen assumes.

**Libertarians** accept the argument and conclude that determinism is false. But they must explain how indeterminism helps. Two approaches dominate.

**Agent causation**, defended by Thomas Reid and, in the twentieth century, by Roderick Chisholm ("Human Freedom and the Self," 1964), holds that free actions are caused not by prior events but by the agent herself, as a substance. When you choose, *you* bring it about, and nothing caused you to do so. Critics ask what kind of causation this is, and whether it fits with a scientific picture of the world.

**Event-causal libertarianism**, developed most fully by Robert Kane (*The Significance of Free Will*, 1996), places indeterminism inside the ordinary causal process of deliberation. Kane focuses on **self-forming actions**: moments of inner conflict, such as when a businesswoman on her way to a meeting witnesses an assault and struggles between helping and hurrying on. Her brain, Kane suggests, is working on both options, with indeterminism making the outcome open. Whichever way she decides, she has made it happen through her own effort, and these choices shape her character, so that later actions flowing from that character are free too.

The central objection to all libertarian views is the **luck objection**. If a choice is undetermined, then two agents identical in every respect up to the moment of choice could choose differently. Imagine replaying the moment of choice a hundred times: sometimes she helps, sometimes she hurries on. What determines which? Nothing about her. Then the outcome seems to be a matter of luck, which seems less, not more, like control. Libertarians reply that the agent is not a bystander to the indeterminism; her efforts are what produce the outcome, either way.

sections.heading: Compatibilism and Frankfurt's Challenge
sections.body:
Compatibilists argue that free will does not require escaping causation. It requires the right kind of causation.

**Classical compatibilism** (Hobbes, Hume) defined freedom as the ability to act as you will, without external constraint. Hume (Day 49) distinguished the liberty of **spontaneity**, acting from your own desires rather than under force, from the liberty of **indifference**, the absence of causes. Only the first, he argued, matters, and it is perfectly compatible with determinism. The prisoner in chains is unfree; the person who chooses tea because she likes it is free, even if her liking was caused.

The classical view was usually combined with a **conditional analysis** of "could have done otherwise": you could have done otherwise if you *would* have done otherwise *had you chosen to*. Under determinism, this remains true. Critics objected: what if you *could not* have chosen otherwise? A person with an irresistible phobia of blood "would have" helped the injured stranger had she chosen to, yet she could not choose to.

In 1969 Harry Frankfurt changed the debate with "Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility." He attacked the **Principle of Alternate Possibilities** (PAP): a person is morally responsible for what they have done only if they could have done otherwise. Frankfurt's counterexample goes like this. Black, a neuroscientist, wants Jones to perform some action, say, to vote for a certain candidate. Black has secretly implanted a device in Jones's brain. If Jones shows any sign of deciding to vote otherwise, Black's device will intervene and make him vote as Black wants. But as it happens, Jones decides on his own to vote for that candidate, for his own reasons. The device never activates.

Is Jones responsible for his vote? It seems so: he did it entirely on his own. Yet he could not have done otherwise. So PAP is false. Moral responsibility depends not on alternative possibilities but on *how* the action actually came about: whether it flowed from the agent's own reasons and will.

If Frankfurt is right, the Consequence Argument may show that determinism rules out alternative possibilities, but that may not matter for responsibility. Libertarians have replied, in a large literature, that in an indeterministic world Black could not know in advance what Jones would decide without some prior sign, which reopens a small but significant alternative.

Frankfurt's second contribution was a positive theory of free will. In "Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person" (1971), he distinguished **first-order desires** (desires to do things, like a desire for a cigarette) from **second-order desires** (desires about which desires to have, or which to act on). His example is the **unwilling addict**: he craves the drug, but he wants that craving not to move him. When it does, he acts unfreely, as a passive bystander to his own desire. A person acts with free will when the desire that moves him is one he wants to be effective: when his will is the will he wants. This **hierarchical theory** is compatible with determinism: what matters is the structure of the will, not its causal origins.

sections.heading: Free Will Skepticism and the Manipulation Argument
sections.body:
Free will skeptics argue that neither libertarians nor compatibilists can deliver the control needed for **basic desert**: deserving blame or praise just because of what one did, regardless of consequences.

Derk Pereboom's **four-case manipulation argument** (*Living Without Free Will*, 2001) is the most discussed challenge to compatibilism. In Case 1, Professor Plum is manipulated moment to moment by neuroscientists, via radio, to kill White, although all compatibilist conditions are met: he acts on his own reasons, his second-order desires endorse his first-order ones, and so on. Most people judge Plum not responsible. In Case 2, he was programmed at the beginning of his life to reason this way. In Case 3, he was conditioned by his upbringing. In Case 4, he is simply a normal person in a deterministic world. Pereboom argues that there is no relevant difference between neighboring cases, so if Plum is not responsible in Case 1, he is not responsible in Case 4, and compatibilism fails.

Compatibilists respond in two ways. **Hard-liners** (Michael McKenna) argue that in Case 1, Plum is responsible after all, so the chain does not support skepticism. **Soft-liners** find a relevant difference: manipulation by another agent who designed the outcome bypasses the person's agency in a way that ordinary causation does not.

Galen Strawson offered another argument, the **Basic Argument**: to be truly responsible for what you do, you must be responsible for how you are, since what you do flows from how you are. But to be responsible for how you are, you must have chosen it, which requires that you already had some character to choose from, and so on in a regress. True self-creation, Strawson concluded, is impossible.

Skeptics do not think everything is permitted. Pereboom argues that we can keep forward-looking practices: protecting society from dangerous people (on a model of quarantine rather than retribution), moral education, and even forms of love and gratitude that do not presuppose desert. Daniel Dennett (*Elbow Room*, 1984; *Freedom Evolves*, 2003) replied that the free will worth wanting is the evolved capacity to deliberate, foresee consequences and respond to reasons, which we really have, determinism or not.

sections.heading: Libet and the Neuroscience of Choice
sections.body:
In 1983 the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet and colleagues published an experiment that has dominated popular discussions of free will ever since. Participants were asked to flex their wrist whenever they felt the urge to, while watching a fast-moving clock and noting the clock position when they first became aware of the urge. Meanwhile, electrodes recorded a slow buildup of electrical activity in the brain known as the **readiness potential**.

The result: the readiness potential began, on average, roughly half a second before the movement, while participants reported becoming aware of their intention only about 200 milliseconds before the movement. The brain, it seemed, had "decided" several hundred milliseconds before the person was aware of deciding. Later studies, such as one by Chun Siong Soon, John-Dylan Haynes and colleagues (2008), used brain imaging to predict which of two buttons people would press, up to several seconds before they reported deciding, though with accuracy only modestly above chance (around 60 percent).

Many concluded that conscious will is an illusion, a view defended by the psychologist Daniel Wegner (*The Illusion of Conscious Will*, 2002). But philosophers and neuroscientists have raised serious objections.
- **What was decided?** The participants had already decided to flex at some point during the experiment. The readiness potential might reflect general preparation, not a decision to move now. Libet himself suggested we retain a "veto" power to cancel actions, sometimes called "free won't."
- **The readiness potential may not be a decision at all.** Aaron Schurger and colleagues (2012) showed that the readiness potential can be modeled as the accumulation of random neural noise, which crosses a threshold and triggers movement. On this interpretation, its early rise is an artifact of averaging trials, not evidence of an unconscious decision.
- **Timing reports are unreliable.** Judging the moment of awareness by watching a clock is notoriously difficult and subject to bias.
- **Trivial choices.** Flexing a wrist at a random moment is not the kind of deliberate, reasons-responsive choice that matters for responsibility. Choosing a career, or whether to tell the truth, is very different.
- **Unconscious does not mean unfree.** Even if decisions begin unconsciously, they are still processes in *your* brain. A compatibilist will point out that the experiments show that decisions have causes, which compatibilists already accepted.

The experiments are valuable, and they have prompted research into how intentions form. But they do not settle a debate that turns, ultimately, on what free will *is*.

modernConnection.title: Free Will in the Courtroom and the Clinic
modernConnection.body:
In 2023 the Stanford neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky published *Determined*, arguing that there is no free will at all and that our legal and moral practices, built on blame and desert, should be transformed accordingly. His case draws not on Libet but on the vast range of factors, from hormones and genes to childhood adversity and culture, that shape behavior. The book reached a large audience and revived an old question in a practical form: if neuroscience explains why someone committed a crime, should they be punished?

Courts already face this question. In the United States, evidence about brain abnormalities, trauma and neurodevelopment is increasingly introduced, especially at sentencing. In *Roper v. Simmons* (2005), which ended the death penalty for crimes committed under the age of 18, the Supreme Court relied on evidence that adolescents are less mature, more impulsive and more vulnerable to outside pressure. Neuroscience did not prove that teenagers lack free will; it supported a compatibilist-style conclusion that their capacities for reasons-responsive control are diminished, and therefore so is their culpability.

This is the distinction that matters. Hard determinists like Sapolsky argue that all behavior is equally caused, so the line between a teenager and an adult, or between a person with a brain tumor and one without, is not a line between unfree and free. Compatibilists reply that what matters is not whether behavior has causes but whether the person has the capacity to recognize and respond to reasons. A brain tumor that destroys impulse control undermines that capacity; an ordinary upbringing does not.

The stakes are also clinical. Addiction medicine is shaped by Frankfurt's unwilling addict: someone who wants to stop but cannot is helped by treatments that restore control, not by blame alone. And a free will skeptic's quarantine model, protecting society without retribution, resembles the rehabilitation-focused prison systems of some Nordic countries. Whatever your view of determinism, these practical debates show how much depends on getting the concepts right.

vocabulary.definition: The thesis that the state of the world at one time, together with the laws of nature, fixes a unique future.
vocabulary.example: If determinism is true, Laplace's demon could predict your next breakfast from the state of the universe at the Big Bang.

vocabulary.definition: The view that free will and moral responsibility are compatible with determinism.
vocabulary.example: A compatibilist says you choose freely when your choice flows from your own reasons, even if those reasons were caused.

vocabulary.definition: The view that we have free will and that this requires that determinism is false.
vocabulary.example: A libertarian holds that, at the moment of choice, more than one future was genuinely open to you.

vocabulary.definition: Van Inwagen's argument that if determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the remote past and the laws of nature, over which we have no choice.
vocabulary.example: The Consequence Argument claims that you can no more change your next decision than the events before your birth.

vocabulary.definition: The principle that a person is morally responsible for an act only if they could have done otherwise.
vocabulary.example: Frankfurt cases are designed to refute the Principle of Alternate Possibilities.

vocabulary.definition: A desire about one's own desires: a desire to have, or to act on, a particular first-order desire.
vocabulary.example: A smoker who wishes she did not crave cigarettes has a second-order desire.

vocabulary.definition: The objection that undetermined choices would be a matter of chance rather than of the agent's control.
vocabulary.example: The luck objection asks what makes an undetermined choice yours rather than a random event in your brain.

vocabulary.definition: A gradual buildup of electrical activity in the brain that precedes voluntary movements, measured in the Libet experiments.
vocabulary.example: The readiness potential began before participants reported being aware of their urge to move.

thinkingExercise.title: Test Your Intuitions Case by Case
thinkingExercise.prompt: Work through Pereboom's cases and a real decision of your own to locate yourself on the map.
steps: Recall a significant decision you made recently. List the factors that caused you to choose as you did (desires, beliefs, habits, upbringing).
Ask whether your decision was free in Hume's sense, in Frankfurt's hierarchical sense, and in the libertarian sense. Which senses does it satisfy?
Read Pereboom's four cases slowly. At which case, if any, do you first judge that Plum is responsible? Write down why the line falls there.
Explain to a friend, in under 150 words, why the Libet experiments do not settle the free will debate.
Decide whether your view requires changing how you blame others or yourself. Write one concrete change you would make, or explain why none is needed.

summary: Determinism says the past and the laws fix a unique future; it differs from fatalism and from predictability. Incompatibilists (hard determinists and libertarians) and compatibilists disagree about whether it rules out free will.
Van Inwagen's Consequence Argument supports incompatibilism; libertarians answer with agent causation or Kane's self-forming actions, but face the luck objection.

Compatibilists define freedom in terms of acting from one's own will; Frankfurt cases attack the Principle of Alternate Possibilities, and Frankfurt's hierarchical theory locates freedom in the structure of desires.
Free will skeptics argue, via Pereboom's manipulation cases and Galen Strawson's Basic Argument, that no one deserves blame in the basic sense, while keeping forward-looking practices.

The Libet experiments found brain activity preceding reported awareness of intentions, but questions about what was decided, the nature of the readiness potential, timing reports and trivial choices mean they do not settle the debate.

quiz.question: How does determinism differ from fatalism?
options: Determinism says the future is unknowable
Fatalism says choices have causes
They are the same view
Determinism says your choices are causal links that make a difference; fatalism says the outcome will happen whatever you do
quiz.explanation: Under determinism, your choices are part of how the future comes about; fatalism says it will come about regardless.

quiz.question: Which premise of the Consequence Argument do compatibilists most often reject?
options: We have no choice about the remote past
The transfer principle that powerlessness carries along chains of consequences
We have no choice about the laws of nature
Determinism concerns the laws of nature
quiz.explanation: The transfer principle (Rule Beta) is the argument's most contested step.

quiz.question: According to the luck objection, if a choice is undetermined, then replaying the same situation could yield different choices with nothing about the agent explaining the difference.
quiz.explanation: This makes undetermined choices seem like chance rather than control, which is the central worry for libertarians.

quiz.question: In a Frankfurt case, Black's device would force Jones to vote for a candidate, but Jones votes for that candidate on his own. What is this meant to show?
options: That moral responsibility does not require the ability to do otherwise
That determinism is false
That Jones is not responsible
That Black is responsible
quiz.explanation: Jones seems responsible though he could not have done otherwise, so the Principle of Alternate Possibilities appears false.

quiz.question: Frankfurt's unwilling addict acts unfreely because:
options: His desire was caused
He has no second-order desires
He is moved by a first-order desire he does not want to be moved by
He could have done otherwise
quiz.explanation: On Frankfurt's hierarchical theory, freedom of the will consists in being moved by desires one endorses at the second order.

quiz.question: Pereboom's four-case argument is designed to show that there is no relevant difference between manipulation and ordinary determinism, so that compatibilism fails.
quiz.explanation: If Plum is not responsible when manipulated and the cases differ in no relevant way, he is not responsible in a merely deterministic world either.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest reason to doubt that the Libet experiments disprove free will?
options: The experiments used too few clocks
Libet was not a neuroscientist
The readiness potential does not exist
The readiness potential may reflect general preparation or neural noise rather than a decision, and the choices were trivial
quiz.explanation: Schurger's model and the nature of the task suggest the readiness potential is not evidence of an unconscious decision about a meaningful choice.

quiz.question: Most professional philosophers in the 2020 PhilPapers survey accepted or leaned toward libertarianism about free will.
quiz.explanation: Compatibilism was the majority view, at around 59 percent.

quiz.question: A court reduces a sentence because the defendant's brain tumor destroyed his impulse control. Which view explains this most naturally?
options: A compatibilist view on which responsibility depends on the capacity to respond to reasons
Fatalism
Agent causation
The view that all behavior is equally unfree
quiz.explanation: Compatibilists distinguish people whose capacity to respond to reasons is impaired from those whose behavior merely has causes.

goDeeper.body:
A sophisticated compatibilist account is the **reasons-responsiveness** theory of John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza (*Responsibility and Control*, 1998). Taking Frankfurt cases seriously, they distinguish two kinds of control. **Regulative control** is the ability to choose between genuinely open alternatives; Frankfurt cases suggest that responsibility does not require it. **Guidance control** is the control you exercise when your action issues from your own mechanism of deliberation, and that mechanism is **moderately reasons-responsive**: it would recognize and respond to sufficient reasons to do otherwise in a range of situations, in an understandable pattern. Jones in the Frankfurt case has guidance control, since his own reasons-responsive mechanism produced the vote, even though Black removed his regulative control.

Fischer and Ravizza also add an **ownership** condition: the mechanism must be one the agent has taken responsibility for, through a history of seeing themselves as an agent whose choices have effects and who is an apt target of reactive attitudes. This historical element is meant to answer manipulation cases: a mechanism implanted by a manipulator is not one the agent has come to own.

On the libertarian side, the **semicompatibilist** move is challenged by Christopher Evan Franklin and others who argue that event-causal libertarianism, carefully stated, adds exactly what compatibilism lacks: a guarantee that the agent's own reasons are the last word. Meanwhile, Christian List (*Why Free Will Is Real*, 2019) has argued that free will exists at the level of agency, a higher level of description, even if determinism holds at the physical level, because indeterminism can exist at the agential level. This **levels** approach connects the free will debate to functionalism (Lesson 1): perhaps choice, like a mental state, is defined at a level of organization above the microphysical.

readings.title: Four Views on Free Will
readings.author: John Martin Fischer, Robert Kane, Derk Pereboom and Manuel Vargas
readings.note: Each author defends a different position and replies to the others; an ideal starting point.

readings.author: Harry Frankfurt
readings.note: The 1971 paper introducing second-order desires and the unwilling addict.

readings.author: Thomas Pink
readings.note: A brisk, opinionated overview with a sympathetic account of libertarianism.

readings.author: Daniel Dennett
readings.note: A witty compatibilist defense of 'the varieties of free will worth wanting'.

questions: Would discovering that determinism is true change how you treat people who wrong you?
Is there any difference that matters between being manipulated by a neuroscientist and being shaped by your upbringing?
Should the criminal justice system be based on desert, on protection, or on rehabilitation?
